title: The 9.O-O-O line: ...d5, the Nxd4 trades and the 9.g4 alternative
question: When White castles at once (9.O-O-O), why can Black play ...d5, and how do the lines 9...d5, 9...Nxd4 and the sharper 9.g4 differ in what they ask of each side?
outcomes: Counts the attackers and defenders of d5 after ...d5 and uses the count to say whether the break works
Names the three ways ...d5 fails here (extra attacker, queen away or blocked, knight chased by g5) and shows each on a board
Steps through 9...d5 10.exd5 Nxd5 11.Nxc6 bxc6 12.Bd4 and says what each move prepares
Chooses the right recapture after ...Nxd4 and avoids the queen recapture, with the engine evidence
Reads game counts as results with a sample size, not as verdicts, and tells a tested claim from a conjecture

steps.text: **The idea: count the recapture.** A pawn break works only if you can answer the trade. A useful first test [I]: after the exchange on d5, count the attackers and defenders of the square and see which pieces do the defending. Here the queen defends the knight down the open d-file. Three failures show up: an extra attacker (the bishop on c4), a missing defender (queen away or blocked), or the knight chased off first (g4-g5). The rook edit later shows a fourth we cannot yet explain.

steps.text: **Answering the opening question.** With the bishop not on c4, nothing hits d5, so the pawn trade stands. The trade opens the d-file and the dragon bishop's long diagonal, and both point at White's king on c1. [I] White cannot close those lines quickly, which is why this break suits a king on the queenside. It is my reading, not an engine verdict.

steps.text: **What the structure asks.** After the knight trade Black has pawns on a7 and c6 with no neighbours, but the b-file is half open for Black and the bishop on c8 is free. White's plans [I]: attack the weak pawns, keep the king safe on c1, play for the better minor pieces. Black's plans [I]: use the half-open b-file, trade queens early to reach an endgame, aim for ...e5 to free the position. These are ideas to test, not verdicts.

steps.text: **The sharper try: 9.g4.** White does not castle yet. The pawn on g4 is guarded by f3 and prepares g5 to chase the knight that guards Black's king. steps.text: **Why it works, when it fails.** Against castling long the queen answers the trade on d5, and no bishop attacks d5. The break also removes White's e-pawn: Nimzowitsch taught that a free, mobile enemy centre pawn should be removed by a prepared break or restrained [V-sheet]. It fails with an extra attacker, a chased knight or a queen that cannot see d5. The rook edit shows a fourth way we cannot explain [H]. Predict first.

**Recap.**
- ...d5 needs the recapture: count attackers and defenders on d5 (a first test [I]).
- It fails against an extra attacker, a blocked queen or a chased knight; the rook edit shows a fourth failure we cannot explain [H].
- After the knight trade Black has isolated a- and c-pawns and the half-open b-file.
- ...Nxd4 is playable but rare: 11 games [V].
- Against the g-pawn push Black plays ...Be6, ...Nxd4 or ...h5.
- Counts show what was played, not what is best.
